column6: Ground plan of a snow house of the Davis Strait tribes
column7: Boas's ground plan of a Cumberland Sound snow house, showing the main dome, the bench, and the entrance formed by two or three small vaults through which a person must crawl. It is the baseline plan against which the excavated Thule winter houses of the same coast are read.

column6: Sections of a Davis Strait snow house
column7: Two sections through the same snow house, showing the two-and-a-half-foot bank of snow raised in the rear half and along both sides of the door and cut off straight, which is the sleeping platform.

column6: Section and interior of a snow house
column7: A cutaway showing the vault lined with skins, the lamp and its drying frame, and the family on the rear bench. Boas notes the lining was frequently made from the cover of the summer tent.

column6: Plan of a double snow house
column7: The plan of a snow house occupied by two families, each woman with her own lamp and her own place on the ledge in front of it.

column6: Plan of an Iglulik house, after Parry
column7: Boas's copy of William Edward Parry's 1823 plan of an Iglulik snow house, reproduced from Parry's second voyage, p. 500. It carries a plan of the same tradition recorded sixty years before Boas's own fieldwork.

column6: Plan of a Hudson Bay house, after Hall
column7: Boas's copy of Charles Francis Hall's plan of a Hudson Bay snow house, one of the northern variants he sets beside the Cumberland Sound form.

column6: Plan and sections of a qarmang or stone house
column7: The plan and two sections of a qarmang, the stone-walled winter house, with the long stone entrance passage or kateng that Boas says ran fifteen to twenty feet in the houses in good condition. The qarmang is the house form the Thule people built and the one archaeologists excavate on this coast.

column6: Plan of a large qarmang for three families
column7: A three-family stone house with a small side room, the qareang, built of poles and bones with a sewn skin ceiling.

column6: Plan of a stone house at Anarnitung, Cumberland Sound
column7: A plan of one of the Anarnitung stone houses, from a drawing by Ludwig Kumlien. Boas notes that at Anarnitung he observed no entrance passage at all, the walls being entirely above ground.

column6: Plan of a group of stone houses at Pangnirtung, Cumberland Sound
column7: Boas's plan of a cluster of qarmat at Pangnirtung, showing how the houses of a settlement stood together.

column6: Plan and sections of a qarmang built of whale ribs
column7: A winter house whose walls are made entirely of whale ribs and jaws, roofed and banked with turf. The whalebone house is the type site of Thule culture across the eastern Arctic.

column6: A storehouse at Ukiadliving
column7: Boas's own sketch of a raised stone storehouse or cache at Ukiadliving, one of a number he found among the qarmat there.

column6: Plan and sections of a tupiq or skin tent of Cumberland Sound
column7: The summer tent of Cumberland Sound, its framework of poles and its skin cover, in plan and section.

column6: Plan and sections of a tupiq of Pond Bay
column7: The tent form used at Mittimatalik (Pond Inlet), in Admiralty Inlet and at Iglulik, where wood is scarce and the frame is built differently from the Cumberland Sound pattern.

column6: Plan and sections of a double winter tent, Cumberland Sound
column7: The banked and doubled summer tent that some families used through the winter in place of a snow house or a stone house.

column6: Interior of a qaggi or singing house of the eastern tribes
column7: A diagram of the large snow house built for singing and drum-dancing, the qaggi, among the eastern tribes.

column6: Plan of a Hudson Bay qaggi, after Hall
column7: Boas's copy of Charles Francis Hall's plan of a Hudson Bay singing house.

column6: Plans of stone foundations Parry took for singing houses
column7: Boas's copy of the stone foundations William Edward Parry recorded near Iglulik and read as the remains of qaggin. They are archaeological features, planned in 1823 and reproduced here.

column6: An old ivory snow goggle found at Idjorituaqtuin, Cumberland Sound
column7: A pre-contact snow goggle of ivory, excavated at Idjorituaqtuin in Cumberland Sound, set beside the modern wooden form. One of the few pieces in Boas's book that is explicitly an archaeological find rather than a collected modern tool.

column6: Flint arrowheads from old graves
column7: Chipped stone arrowheads taken from old graves, now in the National Museum, Washington. Chipped stone of this kind is one of the traits that separates the earlier occupations of the eastern Arctic from the Thule assemblages dominated by ground slate.

column6: An old ulo with a slate blade
column7: The older form of the woman's knife, with a ground slate blade, set beside the modern iron-bladed form. Ground slate is the diagnostic Thule material.

column6: Fragment of an ulo blade of ground slate
column7: A broken ground-slate blade of an ulo, the single commonest find in a Thule house floor.

column6: An ancient tokang or harpoon head
column7: A harpoon head of an older style than any then in use, whose provenance Boas could not establish. Harpoon head typology is what dates a site on this coast.

column6: An old style naulang or harpoon head
column7: The older form of the harpoon head, before iron, which the men carried on all their winter excursions.

column6: Model of a lamp from a grave in Cumberland Sound
column7: A model of a soapstone lamp taken from a grave in Cumberland Sound, one of the grave goods Boas describes with the burial customs.

column6: A qamuting or sledge
column7: The sledge Boas calls the best model, made by the tribes of Hudson Strait and Davis Strait where driftwood is abundant enough for long runners.

column6: Cumberland Sound and Frobisher Bay, drawn by Itu, a Nugumio
column7: A map of Cumberland Sound and Frobisher Bay drawn for Boas by Itu, a Nugumio, and kept in the Museum fuer Voelkerkunde in Berlin. It is Inuit cartography, drawn from memory of the coast, and it is one of the reasons the archaeology of this coast can be tied to named places.

column6: Cumberland Sound and Frobisher Bay, drawn by Sunapignang, an Oqomio
column7: A second Inuit-drawn map of the same coast, by Sunapignang, an Oqomio, to be read against Itu's.

column6: The peninsula of Qivitung, drawn by Angutuqdjuaq, a Padlimio
column7: A map of the Qivitung peninsula drawn for Boas by Angutuqdjuaq, a Padlimio.
